body.p: A yes/no question has exactly the same words and order as the statement. Only the voice rises at the end.

ex.en: You are tired. — Are you tired?

ex.el: Ο Νίκος μένει εδώ. — Ο Νίκος μένει εδώ;
ex.en: Nikos lives here. — Does Nikos live here?

body.p: The subject often moves after the verb, as in a statement with new information: **Μένει εδώ ο Νίκος;** Both orders are correct.
Answers: **Ναι** "yes", **Όχι** "no", **Βέβαια / Φυσικά** "of course", **Μάλιστα** "yes (polite, formal)", **Μπα** "nah, I don't think so", **Ίσως** "maybe".

body.tip: The Greek question mark is **;**. Greek semicolon is a raised dot **·**.

check.why: No auxiliary; the Greek question mark is ;

check.q: Turn into a question: Η Ελένη είναι εδώ.

body.p: **Ποιος** and **πόσος** decline and agree like adjectives: **Ποιον είδες;** "Whom did you see?", **Ποιανού είναι το κλειδί;** "Whose is the key?" (= **Τίνος είναι;**), **Πόσες μέρες θα μείνεις;** "How many days will you stay?" **Τι** never changes: **Τι ώρα είναι; Τι χρώμα θέλεις;**
The question word goes **first**; the subject usually follows the verb: **Πού δουλεύει η Μαρία;**

body.tip: **Πού** "where?" and **πώς** "how?" carry an accent; **που** "who, that" and **πως** "that" do not.

check.why: πόσος agrees with αδέρφια (neuter plural): πόσα.
The object takes the accusative: ποιον.

sections.title: Prepositions move with the question word

body.p: A preposition always stands **directly before** its question word at the front of the question. English leaves it at the end ("Who are you waiting for?"); Greek never does.

ex.en: How (by what) do you get to work?
Who did you give it to?

body.p: **Πού** means "where to" as well as "where", so **Πού πας;** "Where are you going (to)?" needs no preposition.

check.why: The preposition goes with τι at the front.
σε + ποιον first, then the pronoun and the verb.

body.p: **Ή** offers a choice: **Θέλεις τσάι ή καφέ;** **Έρχεσαι ή όχι;** "Are you coming or not?"
A **tag** asks for agreement. Greek uses a few fixed tags instead of English "isn't it, don't you, haven't they":

check.why: Greek uses fixed tags such as ε; or έτσι δεν είναι;
The tag έτσι; at the end.

sections.title: Questions with attitude: μήπως, άραγε, δηλαδή

list: **Μήπως** "by any chance, perhaps": polite or cautious questions, suggestions and worries. **Μήπως είδατε ένα κόκκινο πορτοφόλι;** "Did you by any chance see a red wallet?" **Μήπως να φύγουμε;** "Shall we perhaps leave?"
**Άραγε** "I wonder": questions you ask yourself. **Τι να κάνει άραγε ο Γιώργος;** "I wonder what Giorgos is up to."
**Δηλαδή** "so, that is?": asking for clarification or showing surprise. **Δηλαδή δεν έρχεσαι;** "So you're not coming?"
**Καλά, ...;** expresses disbelief: **Καλά, δεν το ήξερες;** "Seriously, you didn't know?"

body.p: **Τι να + subjunctive** asks "what should I/we ...?": **Τι να κάνουμε;** "What can we do?", **Πού να πάω;** "Where should I go?" The same form is used for rhetorical questions: **Τι να σου πω;** "What can I tell you?"

ex.en: Do you happen to have a pen?
I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.
So I have to start again?
What can I say, I don't know.

check.q: You stop a stranger politely: "Do you happen to know the time?"
check.why: Μήπως + polite plural is the courteous form.
δηλαδή asks for confirmation of a surprising conclusion.

body.p: **Να** + noun points at something with surprise: **Να ο Νίκος!** "There's Nikos!" **Να τα μας!** "Here we go again!"
**Και τι έγινε;** "So what?" and **Τι λες!** "You don't say!" are fixed exclamatory questions.

An **indirect question** depends on a verb such as **ρωτάω, ξέρω, αναρωτιέμαι, δεν καταλαβαίνω**. The question word stays and the question mark goes. Yes/no questions take **αν** "if, whether" or **μήπως**.

ex.en: I don't know what to do.
Ask him if he happens to know.

body.p: Note **τι να + subjunctive** for "what to do", **πού να** "where to", **πώς να** "how to": Greek has no infinitive.

A **rhetorical question** states the opposite of what it asks: **Ποιος δεν θέλει να είναι ευτυχισμένος;** "Who doesn't want to be happy?" (= everybody does). **Τι να κάνουμε;** "What can we do?" (= nothing). In essays they open a paragraph or close an argument; use them sparingly.

The question word stays, the question mark goes.

title: Questions and exclamations
blurb: Yes/no questions by intonation, question words and their order, μήπως and άραγε, tag questions, choice questions, and exclamations with τι, πόσο and να.

intro.p: Greek questions are simple in form: there is no "do" and no change of order for a yes/no question, only rising intonation and the Greek question mark **;** (it looks like an English semicolon). The question words come first, prepositions travel with them, and a handful of particles (**μήπως, άραγε, δηλαδή, ε**) give a question its attitude. Exclamations reuse the question words **τι** and **πόσο**.
